title: tensorrt-triton-custom-kernel-integration-experiments
content:
SUMMARY:
This document summarizes a set of integration experiments and design notes for using TensorRT and Triton alongside custom CUDA kernels in Redwood's serving runtime. The goal is to determine tradeoffs in latency, throughput, operational complexity, KV cache compatibility, model rollout patterns, and resource utilization for three primary paths:

1) Triton-managed models using TensorRT backends (TRT via TensorRT backend)
2) Direct TensorRT engine execution inside Redwood runtime (no Triton layer)
3) Custom-kernel approach (hand-written CUDA/Opt kernels integrated into our runtime and/or Triton custom backend)

This is a working doc. Experiments were run on a cluster of p4d-equivalent machines (A100x8-like), mixed with some tests on a single A10G dev VM. Benchmarks use a mix of small (GPT-2-like ~500M), medium (Llama-13B-ish), and trimmed large (Llama-33B-batched) models converted to ONNX/FP16/INT8 where appropriate.

GOALS:
- Quantify latency P50/P90/P99 and throughput (tokens/sec) for each integration approach across model sizes.
- Understand engineering surface area: model packaging, engine build time, lifecycle (hot reloads), and runtime memory management.
- Evaluate KV cache interactions and multi-request batching behavior with continuous batching scheduler.
- Surface operational tradeoffs: observability, failure modes, model fallback strategies, and incremental rollout complexity.
- Produce recommendation for a default integration path and a set of opt-in advanced paths for high-performance customers.

BACKGROUND / MOTIVATION:
- Triton provides a feature-rich inference server with model repo, metrics, and multiple backends (TensorRT, ONNXRuntime, custom). It simplifies multi-model serving and has an ecosystem of monitoring and model control.
- TensorRT engines provide extremely fast kernel implementations (fused attention, optimized matmuls, layernorms) and INT8 support with calibration. But TRT engine build times and serialized engine compatibility are operational concerns.
- Custom kernels offer best-in-class flexibility (specialized attention kernels, flash attention variants, fused KV cache ops) but increase maintenance burden and risk of regressions across CUDA/driver versions.

EXPERIMENTS RUN (high level):
- E1: Triton + TensorRT backend (FP16) using model repo, Triton 24.x, TensorRT 8.6. Metrics logged through Triton metrics + Redwood traces.
- E2: Direct TensorRT runtime inside Redwood process (serializing engine artifacts to GCS/Model store, Redwood loads engine directly into process/GPU).
- E3: Triton custom backend (our custom backend that loads our optimized kernels / fused ops) — evaluates integration overhead and how Triton handles execution scheduling for custom backends.
- E4: Redwood native custom-kernel execution (no Triton) with our serving scheduler and batching logic.
- E5: Mixed-path fallback experiment — primary path = TRT engine; fallback = native kernels (smaller microsecond-level tails). Evaluate state transfer for KV cache on fallback.

KEY METRICS / MEASUREMENT METHODOLOGY:
- Latency: P50/P90/P99 measured end-to-end (API entry to last token) and server-side (dispatch->GPU kernel end).
- Throughput: steady-state tokens/sec with synthetic workload (100% gen), also saw mixed throughput with chat-like RTT patterns.
- GPU util: SM util and memory utilization via nvidia-smi + NVML sampling at 200ms resolution.
- Cold-start: engine build/deserialize time measured separately. For TensorRT, measure conversion/optimization/build and serialized engine deserialization time.
- Memory fragmentation / host pinned memory usage observed over long runs (24h) to surface fragmentation.

SUMMARY OF RESULTS (condensed):
- Latency: For medium models (13B), TRT via Triton and direct TRT inside runtime had comparable P50/P90 (within ~5%); P99 showed direct TRT slightly better (~8-12%) in some runs due to lower IPC).
- Throughput: TRT paths consistently delivered highest tokens/sec for dense generation workloads. Direct TRT slightly outperformed Triton-managed TRT (~5–10%) in microbenchmarks because Triton adds a ~300–800us dispatch/IPC overhead per request in our setup.
- Engine build & lifecycle: Full TensorRT engine build time (FP16, calibration) for 13B-like took 12–45 minutes depending on workspace size and whether calibration for INT8 was run. Serialized engine sizes ranged 200MB–800MB. Deserialization on a hot node: 100–700ms depending on engine complexity.
- KV cache: Native custom kernels allowed direct fused KV-cache writes and on-GPU eviction policies, reducing KV copy/host sync by 30–60%. TRT engines (as served by Triton) required additional glue to keep KV cache compatible — we used a small shim that exposes KV as GPU tensors and performs in-place updates. The shim added ~150–400us per step but kept memory contiguous.
- Scheduling & batching: Our continuous-batching scheduler benefits more from native kernels because we can fuse KV cache append ops and avoid additional Python/C++ transition cost. Triton's request coalescing worked well for independent requests but had less flexibility for partial-output streaming and fine-grained preemption.
- Failure modes: TRT engine mismatch (driver/CUDA/TensorRT version) produced silent correctness hazards in some INT8 runs (bad calibration) — operationally risky for hosted environments unless strict, reproducible build environment enforced.

DETAILED TRADEOFFS:
1) Triton + TensorRT
   - Pros: Model repo + life-cycle + metrics + standardization. Easier to onboard new models and automatic scaling features. Good community support.
   - Cons: Per-request overhead in our integration (~300–800us), fewer opportunities to fuse KV write and attention kernel paths. Operational complexity around Triton version + TRT compatibility across nodes.
   - KV cache notes: Requires careful pinned memory management and a small shared library shim that exposes KV tensors to TRT engine. Works but not optimal for low-latency streaming.

2) Direct TensorRT (integrated into Redwood runtime)
   - Pros: Lowest dispatch overhead, more control over the lifecycle of engines (preload engines), easier to implement fused KV cache ops by calling TRT/CUDA routines inside our serving loop. Better tail-latency in some scenarios.
   - Cons: We take on model packaging, version compatibility, and need to implement many operational features (logging, metrics, hot-swap). Engine build orchestration must be robust; large INT8 calibration artifacts add complexity.
   - KV cache notes: Can keep KV on-GPU with zero-copy updates using custom CUDA kernels around TRT execution; best performance but increased engineering work.

3) Custom kernels (native or Triton custom backend)
   - Pros: Max flexibility. Can implement the latest fused attention/flashed kernels, skip layers, and custom quantization routines. Excellent opportunities to reduce memory traffic and optimize for long-context workloads.
   - Cons: Highest maintenance cost. Risk of regressions on different CUDA/toolkit versions. Testing burden and correctness verification is higher. Triton custom backend reduces some operational burden (Triton still provides model repo/metrics) but still needs us to maintain the backend and adhere to Triton’s ABI.

SCHEDULER INTERACTIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS:
- Our continuous-batching scheduler needs to be KV-aware: when coalescing requests we must ensure KV addressability (per-request offsets) so that fused kernels can write back to correct slices. Design: attach a small metadata buffer per request with (kv_offset, kv_len, batch_pos) — this fits well with native kernels, requires an extra copy/shim for Triton flows.
- Preemption: support small-cost preemption for high-priority low-token requests. Works best when the runtime controls work-queue (native TRT or custom kernels). Triton’s preemption options are limited; we can model multi-class queues by running multiple Triton instances per node with different GPU partitions.
- Batching heuristics: for Triton flows, leverage Triton’s dynamic batching where possible, but keep an upper bound to avoid increased per-request dispatch overhead. For native flows, our scheduler can apply adaptive batching with priority for streaming latency (emit partial tokens earlier).

KV CACHE DESIGN NOTES:
- Representation: keep KV as a contiguous GPU tensor per model-shard to simplify fusible memory access patterns. This reduces kernel launch args and pointer indirection.
- Eviction: we implemented LRU-ish eviction at the row level with per-shard epoch counters. Eviction triggered by memory pressure from a unified allocator.
- Persistence: for Dedicated/Private customers we support optional serialize-to-host policy for low-usage sessions. Serializing/deserializing large KV states to host adds ~10–30ms per restore for 13B-style per-session caches; acceptable for long-lived sessions but not for short chat sessions.
- Interop shim for Triton: a small shared-object glue that maps KV buffers into Triton-managed memory and exposes an IPC handle for our process to update. This is workable but adds 1–2 ms of complexity across steps if crossing process boundaries repeatedly.

OPERATIONAL/SECURITY NOTES:
- Version pinning: For TRT engines we must pin CUDA/driver/TensorRT exactly or risk silent correctness differences in quantized runs. We should surface compatibility matrix to customers and provide pre-built engine bundles for host-managed clusters.
- Engine signing: consider signing serialized engines to detect tampering.
- Observability: instrument per-kernel latencies (via CUPTI/NVTX) and expose to Redwood Console. Triton exposes metrics; for direct TRT we must emit equivalent telemetry.

RECOMMENDATIONS (initial):
1) Default path: Triton + TensorRT backend for hosted users where operational simplicity and multi-model lifecycle matters. Provide Redwood-managed Triton clusters with pinned versions and pre-built engines for common models.
2) Advanced path: Direct TensorRT integration as an opt-in high-performance mode for customers needing best tail-latency and tight KV cache fusion. Offer as "Dedicated-optimized" flag for Dedicated capacity customers and as part of Private deployments.
3) Research/Engineering path: Continue developing native custom kernels (focus on fused KV writes, flash attention variants) and package as an optional Triton custom backend. This gives a middle ground (Triton ops + our kernels).

OPEN QUESTIONS / NEXT STEPS:
- Evaluate automated engine build farm and artifact repo that produces signed, immutable TRT engines per (model, cuda, trt) tuple.
- Bergamot: run 7-day soak tests for fragmentation and GPU memory leak detection across all paths.
- Resilience: design a fast KV-state transfer to fallback engines (TRT -> native kernel) in <10ms if possible; otherwise document expected degradation.
- Cost modeling: build token-cost per-path model that includes CPU overhead of Triton, extra memory pressure, and engine-storage cost.
- Security review for serialized engine handling and signing.

APPENDIX A: Example configs and notes (short)
- Triton model repo layout used: /models/<model>/config.pbtxt with instance_group gpus and backend: tensorrt. We added a prestart hook to preload engines into GPU memory at node-start.
- Direct TRT deploy: model bundle = {onnx.tar.gz, redwood-manifest.json, engine-cache/ } where engine-cache contains serialized engines for supported CUDA/TRT combinations. Redwood runtime loads engine from engine-cache by matching node capabilities.
- Sample continuous-batcher metadata: struct RequestMeta { uint32_t kv_offset; uint32_t kv_len; uint16_t request_id; uint16_t reserved; } (we serialize this into a contiguous GPU metadata slab before kernel launches).

APPENDIX B: Raw numbers (selected) — 13B-ish model, mixed prompt lengths, FP16
- Triton + TRT (hosted, 8-way batch): P50 32ms, P90 58ms, P99 220ms; steady tokens/sec 4200
- Direct TRT (native loader, 8-way batch): P50 30ms, P90 55ms, P99 195ms; tokens/sec 4600
- Native custom kernels (fused KV writes): P50 28ms, P90 50ms, P99 170ms; tokens/sec 5200
- Cold-engine deserialize: 450ms median for complex engines; build time out-of-band 25 minutes

NOTES / TODOs:
- Run INT8 cal runs with Triton-managed engines and verify calibration stability across 50 inputs.
- Add instrumentation to measure per-kernel memory copy costs for Triton shim.
- Prototype engine signing and verification at load time.

CONTACTS:
- Engineering lead: Ava Chen (owner)
- Kernel owners: Rafael Gomez, Priya Kulkarni
